title: DNS over QUIC RFC 9250 EDNS(0) and DNS Message Size Architecture
purpose: Define the DoQ codec behavior for ignoring the EDNS(0) UDP payload size field and enforcing the 65535-byte maximum message size via the 2-octet length prefix.
design_summary: The DoqMessageCodec already implements a 2-octet length prefix whose maximum representable value is ushort.MaxValue (65535). The EDNS(0) UDP payload size field is never read or consulted by the codec; it is present in the OPT pseudo-RR but semantically irrelevant for message-size admission. A new explicit validation in TryDecode confirms the decoded payload length does not exceed MaxPayloadLength (65535). Encode already rejects payloads larger than 65535. Boundary and property-style fuzz tests confirm correct behavior at the limit values and with malformed inputs.
data_and_state_considerations: No new adapter state is required. The codec remains a stateless static helper class.
edge_cases_and_constraints: The length prefix is exactly 2 octets; value 0 is a valid payload length.
TryDecode must accept payload lengths 0 through 65535 inclusive.
TryDecode must not attempt to consult or validate EDNS(0) OPT record fields during message-size admission.
Encode must reject payloads whose length exceeds MaxPayloadLength.
risks: The 65535-byte bound is absolute; the implementation does not support the larger message sizes that EDNS(0) UDP payload size fields could theoretically advertise over TCP transports.

supplemental_sections.heading: Implementation Boundary
supplemental_sections.content: All changes are confined to DoqMessageCodec. The EDNS(0) UDP payload size field is structurally present in DNS OPT records but never evaluated for message-size decisions. No parsing of the DNS body beyond the 2-octet length prefix is required for message-size admission.

supplemental_sections.heading: Rationale
supplemental_sections.content: RFC 9250 section 4.6 specifies that DoQ uses a fixed 65535-byte maximum DNS message size, overriding any EDNS(0) UDP payload size advertisement. The 2-octet length prefix natively enforces this bound because the prefix can represent values 0-65535 only.
